title: Sugriva's apology
hookLine: an apology, armies covering the earth, and kshama
carry: kshama: forgiveness, patient as the earth

cards: Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain.

Sugriva is on his throne, in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.

teach.b: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement.
Sugriva doesn't argue. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped.
Who doesn't? But I'm his friend, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness, forgive me.
He owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action, and Lakshmana softens at once. Come and see Rama, he says.
Sugriva bows before Rama with joined palms, and Rama receives him with an embrace and sits him at his side.
While they talk, the armies arrive: monkeys and bears past counting, from mountains and seashores and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth.

The Sanskrit word for what Rama gives is kshama: forgiveness, and patience, and also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. The Bhagavad Gita lists kshama among the divine qualities a person can grow.
And many Hindus practice it before they're even out of bed.

teach.h: FORGIVE ME FOR TOUCHING YOU WITH MY FEET.
teach.b: A morning prayer to the earth goddess, Bhumi, asks her: forgive me for touching you with my feet. The word for forgive there comes from the same root.

Ask for kshama every morning, and you start learning to give it, from the one who bears everything. It meets a life now in families: someone slips and owns it, and the one let down doesn't keep a ledger.
Rama doesn't hold the lost weeks against him. And then he turns to the real question: where do we look first?

how: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the divine qualities in the Bhagavad Gita (16.3); many Hindus begin the day with a short prayer asking Bhumi, the earth, to forgive the touch of their feet.

o: an order banishing Sugriva from his own city
the rebuke that ends in an apology and an embrace
a duel between Sugriva and Rama's angry brother

p: no atonement for it, says Lakshmana
owns the fault and asks forgiveness
forgiveness, and a name for the earth

s: Sugriva argues that he did nothing wrong
he owns the slip, asks forgiveness, and pledges his army.
Rama receives Sugriva with an embrace
and asks him to sit beside him.
many Hindus ask the earth's forgiveness each morning
a short prayer to Bhumi asks pardon for the touch of their feet.

games.q: a friend who let you down says sorry, and keeps saying it. by Rama's kshama, what fits?
o: let her say it a few more times.
take it and let it go, the way Rama embraced Sugriva.
say it's fine and quietly keep score.
games.why: Sugriva owned his slip and Rama embraced him at once: kshama bears it, like the earth.

practice: Try the old morning gesture: touch the floor with your fingers, then your heart or forehead, asking the earth's pardon for walking on her. If you don't pray, simply touch the floor and say thank you.

Now think of a small fault of yours that someone might still be holding, and own it plainly: yes, I did that. Then think of someone you could forgive, and let your hand rest open on your knee, palm up.

wordCard.voice: Lakshmana's warning. It ends in Sugriva's apology, Rama's embrace, and kshama, patient as the earth.

orig.note: Sanskrit kṣamā: forgiveness, patience, forbearance; also a name for the earth, who bears everything.

carryVoice: Your line: kshama: forgiveness, patient as the earth. A fault owned, and no ledger kept. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 37–39 (the armies gather; Rama embraces Sugriva)
Bhagavad Gita 16.3 (kshama among the divine qualities)
Traditional morning prayer to Bhumi Devi ('samudra-vasane devi… pada-sparsham kshamasva me')
